snippet.title: 'Power Emergency': Blackout Fears Erupt as 20 Million People in 17 States Put On Alert by DOE
snippet.description:
- Blackout fears are growing for 20 million Americans as extreme heat pushes the power grid toward its limits.

The US Department of Energy (DOE) on Sunday authorized the operator serving parts of 17 states to activate idle power sources in an effort to keep the lights on.

The move allows backup plants that are normally switched off to generate extra electricity if surging demand threatens to overwhelm the grid. 

The emergency order covers Arizona, Arkansas, Colorado, Iowa, Kansas, Louisiana, Minnesota, Missouri and Montana. It also includes Nebraska, New Mexico, North Dakota, Oklahoma, South Dakota, Texas, Utah and Wyoming.

The move gives Southwest Power Pool (SPP), which oversees the central US grid, permission to deploy backup generators if electricity supplies become strained.

It is the final step before a Level 3 Energy Emergency Alert, which could trigger rolling blackouts to prevent a wider collapse.

The order will remain in effect through August 3 to 'mitigate the risk of blackouts,' according to the DOE. 

It comes as 40 million Americans face extreme heat warnings, with soaring temperatures and oppressive humidity driving up demand for air conditioning.

Former DOE official Kerry Duggan said extreme heat is increasingly becoming an energy challenge rather than a simple weather event.

'As we experience more frequent and longer-lasting heat waves, our ability to keep homes, businesses and critical facilities cool depends on having a reliable and resilient electric grid,' Duggan said.

National Weather Service's Monday alerts across much of that region forecast temperatures or heat indexes above 100F, with readings reaching 113F to 115F in parts of Louisiana. 

Texas, Arkansas, Oklahoma, Kansas, Colorado and Nebraska were also facing dangerous conditions approaching 110F. 

Meteorologists have blamed the brutal conditions on another heat dome, which traps hot air over a region and causes temperatures to climb for days. 

US Secretary of Energy Chris Wright said: 'The Trump Administration is tapping into an abundant supply of unused backup generation to maintain affordable, reliable, and secure power for hardworking American families and businesses.

'The previous administration's energy subtraction policies weakened the grid, leaving Americans more vulnerable during emergency events. 

'Thanks to President Trump's leadership, we are reversing those failures and using every available tool to ensure Americans have continued access to affordable, reliable, and secure energy to power and cool their homes.' 

DOE estimates that more than 35 gigawatts (GW) of unused backup generation remain available nationwide. 

The ⁠risk of rotating blackouts escalated in SPP in the past week. 

On Friday, a sudden loss of electricity imported from neighboring grids left the utility company with razor-thin reserves for possible power plant outages and falling renewable generation in its territory spanning parts of Arizona, Colorado, Montana, Nebraska, South Dakota, Wyoming and Utah. 

SPP ​avoided outages that day ​by appealing for voluntary ⁠conservation of electricity to maintain reserves. 

But the company expected the western territory's highest demand of the week on Sunday evening as temperatures rose above 90F.

localized.title: 'Power Emergency': Blackout Fears Erupt as 20 Million People in 17 States Put On Alert by DOE
localized.description:
- Blackout fears are growing for 20 million Americans as extreme heat pushes the power grid toward its limits.

The US Department of Energy (DOE) on Sunday authorized the operator serving parts of 17 states to activate idle power sources in an effort to keep the lights on.

The move allows backup plants that are normally switched off to generate extra electricity if surging demand threatens to overwhelm the grid. 

The emergency order covers Arizona, Arkansas, Colorado, Iowa, Kansas, Louisiana, Minnesota, Missouri and Montana. It also includes Nebraska, New Mexico, North Dakota, Oklahoma, South Dakota, Texas, Utah and Wyoming.

The move gives Southwest Power Pool (SPP), which oversees the central US grid, permission to deploy backup generators if electricity supplies become strained.

It is the final step before a Level 3 Energy Emergency Alert, which could trigger rolling blackouts to prevent a wider collapse.

The order will remain in effect through August 3 to 'mitigate the risk of blackouts,' according to the DOE. 

It comes as 40 million Americans face extreme heat warnings, with soaring temperatures and oppressive humidity driving up demand for air conditioning.

Former DOE official Kerry Duggan said extreme heat is increasingly becoming an energy challenge rather than a simple weather event.

'As we experience more frequent and longer-lasting heat waves, our ability to keep homes, businesses and critical facilities cool depends on having a reliable and resilient electric grid,' Duggan said.

National Weather Service's Monday alerts across much of that region forecast temperatures or heat indexes above 100F, with readings reaching 113F to 115F in parts of Louisiana. 

Texas, Arkansas, Oklahoma, Kansas, Colorado and Nebraska were also facing dangerous conditions approaching 110F. 

Meteorologists have blamed the brutal conditions on another heat dome, which traps hot air over a region and causes temperatures to climb for days. 

US Secretary of Energy Chris Wright said: 'The Trump Administration is tapping into an abundant supply of unused backup generation to maintain affordable, reliable, and secure power for hardworking American families and businesses.

'The previous administration's energy subtraction policies weakened the grid, leaving Americans more vulnerable during emergency events. 

'Thanks to President Trump's leadership, we are reversing those failures and using every available tool to ensure Americans have continued access to affordable, reliable, and secure energy to power and cool their homes.' 

DOE estimates that more than 35 gigawatts (GW) of unused backup generation remain available nationwide. 

The ⁠risk of rotating blackouts escalated in SPP in the past week. 

On Friday, a sudden loss of electricity imported from neighboring grids left the utility company with razor-thin reserves for possible power plant outages and falling renewable generation in its territory spanning parts of Arizona, Colorado, Montana, Nebraska, South Dakota, Wyoming and Utah. 

SPP ​avoided outages that day ​by appealing for voluntary ⁠conservation of electricity to maintain reserves. 

But the company expected the western territory's highest demand of the week on Sunday evening as temperatures rose above 90F.

Looking for the ultimate 72-hour survival kit, bug out bag, get-home bag, hiking day pack, emergency kit, or ultralight backpacking setup? After decades of testing survival gear in the real world, I built an ultralight 5-pound survival kit that covers the essentials without unnecessary weight. Whether you’re preparing for emergency preparedness, wilderness survival, backpacking, hiking, camping, overlanding, bushcraft, self-reliance, or simply building a lightweight emergency bag, this minimalist survival kit is designed to maximize capability while minimizing weight.

I am Jason Salyer with On Three Survival and Preparedness. In this video, I break down exactly what I carry, why I carry it, and how decades of real-world experience have refined this lightweight emergency kit. Whether you’re building a bug out bag (BOB), get-home bag (GHB), hiking day pack, emergency go bag, survival backpack, camping kit, vehicle emergency kit, or disaster preparedness kit, these ideas can help you stay prepared without carrying unnecessary weight. I believe preparedness should be practical, affordable, and built around gear that actually works—not hype.

When winter storms knock out power, you have hours - not days - before your home becomes uninhabitable. 

This comprehensive guide covers the 11 essential items that separate prepared families from emergency casualties during winter blackouts.


I'm Zach, and I've been prepping since 2012. After surviving multiple extended winter outages, including a brutal 5-day blackout in Minnesota, I learned these items aren't just recommended, they're absolutely critical for winter survival when the grid goes down.


What You'll Learn:

Alternative cooking methods that work when your stove is dead (and the deadly mistakes most people make)

Water storage and purification systems for when pipes freeze and municipal systems fail

Insulation techniques that turn your home into a thermal fortress

Non-perishable food strategies that go beyond basic canned goods

Manual tools for emergency repairs when power tools are useless

Backup heating solutions that won't kill you with carbon monoxide

Illumination systems for 14+ hours of daily darkness

Communication devices that work when cell towers are down

Sanitation supplies that prevent disease in close quarters

Medical supplies and medications for when help can't reach you

Emergency power generation that keeps critical systems running

Each item includes specific product recommendations, safety protocols, and real-world insights from someone who's actually lived through these situations. 

This isn't theoretical prepping - it's practical survival knowledge that could save your family's life.


Winter power outages are increasing in frequency and duration due to aging infrastructure and extreme weather events. 

The Texas freeze of 2021 left over 4 million people without power in sub-zero temperatures. 

Hundreds died from hypothermia, carbon monoxide poisoning, and preventable accidents that proper preparation would have avoided.
Don't become another statistic. 

These 11 items create a comprehensive foundation for surviving extended winter blackouts with safety and relative comfort.

snippet.description:
Sources: https://tinyurl.com/critical32
Emergency Preparedness Guide: https://payhip.com/b/GWENV
Your support helps us keep covering the planet's natural hazards

The New Madrid Seismic Zone has a problem: the ground records repeated major earthquakes, but GPS instruments measure remarkably little surface strain. The 1811-1812 New Madrid earthquakes shook the central United States, reshaped land around Reelfoot Lake and sent waves up the Mississippi River. If this fault system is preparing for another major earthquake, why is the expected movement so difficult to find?

We will follow the evidence beneath Missouri, Arkansas, Tennessee and Kentucky: buried faults, ancient sand blows, competing GPS studies and the debate over centuries-long aftershocks. We will also cover earthquake preparedness and why calling New Madrid "overdue" turns a complex geological record into a misleading countdown.
